TROUBLE BETWEEN COLORED PEOPLE AND POLICEMEN.
New York Sept. 27. An Atlanta Commercial
NEW YORK, Sept. 27.—An Atlanta, Ga., special in an evening paper states that during the commemoration services at DeGive's Opera House last evening the police keeping back the crowd were assaulted by a colored man, who was soon joined by others, and a general riot became iminent. Twenty-five thousand people lined the streets, and a panic at one time struck them. A scue of the wildest confusion ensued which resulted in the crushing of many children. [Special to the N. O. Democrat.]

ATLANTA, GA., September 26.—The largest crowd ever seen on the streets of Atlanta turned out this afternoon to witness the memorial services, under the auspices of Cœur De Lion, Commandery of the Knights Templar. At least thirty thousand people, more than half of them negroes, were congregated upon Marietta street, when the procession, the largest ever seen here, halted in front of Degire's Opera house where the funeral ceremonies were held. The procession was composed of the Commandery, the Fifth Artillery of the United States, the City Council, a regiment of local military, a battalion of colored military, several lodges of colored Odd Fellows and many other local associations. The Opera House could not accommodate one-tenth of the people, so a large part of the procession remained in the street with the vast concourse during the exercises. The Opera House was beautifully dressed, the black cloth with which the stage and galleries was gracefully hung bearing handsomely worked and bold insignia of the order—a magnificent metallic case surmounted a catafalque in the centre of the stage and to the front in a semi-circle were ranged the principal officers of the stage and to the front in a semi-circle were ranged the principal officers of the lodge. The Fifth Artillery band furnished the music, and fine addresses were spoken by Capt. Henry Jackson and the Revs. D. W. Given and A. G. Thomas. Appropriate resolutions were read and the exercises were closed with the doxology led by the band and choir and joined in by the great audience. While the exercises were progressing up stairs, a colored Odd Fellow, who could not jam his way in, got mad and kicked over a stack of guns, whereupon a soldier of the Fifth Artillery clubbed him with his musket, the negro's friends rallied to him, when the police rushed in, and aided by the Fifth Artillery, prevented a riot. This incident demoralized the crowd, which broke in every direction amid the shrieks of women and the shouts of men. A few moments later a police captain tried to arrest an unruly negro man at the foot of the stairs, when he struck at the officer, missed him, and planted his fist full in the face of a white lady, knocking her flat; thereupon the officer clubbed him tearfully; the soldiers and citizens wounding several negroes in attempting to keep back the crowd. Many arrests were made, and just as the police were entering the station on Pryor street, a negro man threw a large rock, knocking a white man down, near the door, and a crowd of negroes, bent upon rescuing their friends, formed in a line about a square from the station, where they were harangued by a large negro who brandished a huge butcher knife in his right hand, and told them to "carve their way through." Mr. KELLY interposes a seeming denial against the statement of Col. GEORGE BLISS, who says that in 1878 he had dealings with the boss of Tammany.

EDGEFIELD COURTHOUSE, October 31.—Edgefield is in ashes. The business part of the town is totally destroyed, only three stores being left. The Tillman Hotel was consumed. There are not provisions enough left to last twenty-four hours. The office of the Chronicle newspaper was burned. The Advertiser building and property is safe. OUR COUSINS GERMAN

Handsomely Entertained by the Good Folks of Chicago.

CHICAGO, October 31.—The Von Steuben party got an early start this morning, and had a ride about the principal streets with the Mayor and some prominent citizens. At the formal reception and welcome, Mayor Harrison astonished the German visitors by delivering, with some fluency, a speech in their native tongue, the purport of which was that republics are usually ungrateful, yet the services of Baron Von Steuben to this country were so important that gratitude dwelt in the hearts and homes of the people, not only for him, but his descendants. Colonel Von Steuben replied briefly and aptly in German, and Walker Blaine made a brief speech in English in his behalf. At noon the distinguished guests went on Change, and were received with hearty cheers and hand-clapping. The President of the board, Mr. Rogers, welcomed them in a few words. Mayor Harrison and Walker Blaine responded in their behalf, and then the audience tried to draw out Lieutenant-General Sheridan who modestly shook his head, remarking sotto voce to the Mayor, that he would attempt no speech lest he make a bull and displease the bears, a remark which the Mayor repeated to the board, causing much merriment over the wit of the soldier. POLITICAL.

Cannon, of Utah, Declared to Be as Allion.

SALT LAKE, U. T., Oct. 31.—The suit brought by Campbell to annul Cannon's pretended certificate of naturalization was decided today by Chief-Justice Hunter. The Judge held that, on the statements of the complainant and the admissions of the defendant, the certificate of Cannon was void on its face; that the pretended naturalization was a nullity. Thus the court in which Cannon pretends to have been naturalized twenty-five years ago decides that he is an alien, and therefore that Gov. Murray was right in refusing to certify that he had been duly elected to Congress. It is not supposed here that the House of Representatives can fail to take notice of this action, or, indeed, to be governed by it, and thus it is regarded as virtually settling the contest for the Delegate's seat from Utah in favor of Campbell. The Liberal candidates and the Liberals of Utah like tired soldiers at the striking up of music or opening of fire in front, are plucking up new heart in consequence.

BLOODY WORK IN ORANGE
St. Louis, August 23. — The Republican's special from Houston, Texas, received last night, gives particulars of the bloody tragedies, which have occurred at Orange during the week past, and which have been previously mentioned. They have caused intense excitement along the line of the Texas & New Orleans railroad, and fears are entertained that something worse is to follow. The citizens of Orange have risen en masse and are determined to end the reign of lawlessness that has prevailed for the past month. The present condition of affairs grew out of a difficulty which occurred three weeks ago between O. L. Delano, a noted desperado, and a detective named Wood, in which Delano was seriously shot. Wood escaped, and Charles Delano, a brother of O. L., accused the sheriff, Geo. Michael, of aiding in the escape, and swore he would get even with him. With this view he concocted a plan to assassinate Michael, and was aided by Dug Harris and two negroes, Sam and Bob Saxon. The plan failed, but they succeeded in very seriously wounding the sheriff by leading him into an ambush. The citizens became greatly incensed at these proceedings, and 150 of them congregated, captured four of the negroes and shot them. Bob Saxon was also captured, and after extorting a confession from him, in which he reviewed the plot to kill the sheriff and gave much other information, he was hanged to a tree. Another negro was arrested and hanged, and Chas. Delano was captured and placed in jail. A hundred armed men scoured the neighboring swamps for others of the gang.

Great Excitement in Wellington and Caldwell.

President Danford and Cashier Smith Under Arrest.

Sunday morning's Commonwealth contained a special dispatch announcing the suspension of the Danford banks at Wellington and Caldwell in this state. It seems the doors of the two institutions were virtually closed on Friday last—that is, the money ran out that day. The last of it was taken by a depositor who presented a pistol at Cashier Smith's head, and demanded his money. Mr. Smith kept the doors of the Wellington bank open Saturday, and assured all callers that Mr. Danford, the president, who lives at Osage City, would be there that night with enough currency to pay all deposits. Mr. Danford came, but the promised currency was non est. Seeing the excitement that prevailed Danford went over to Wichita. NEWPORT, ARK., September 10.—About two o'clock this morning the jail at Jacksonport was surrounded by a large number of masked men in arms. The keys were demanded of Jailor Lankford, who attempted to run, but was fired upon and captured by the mob. His life was threatened and a rope placed around his neck, still he positively refused to surrender the keys.

The infuriated mob then fell upon the jail doors with hammers, chisels and bars, and in less than ten minutes an entrance was effected. Henry Allen, who stabbed J. E. Williams in Newport on the 7th inst., was dragged to a locust tree near by and hung.

The Circuit Court is now in session, and the citizens, generally, are greatly incensed at the ferocious deed. As to who the participants were, remains a mystery to the public. Williams is still in a serious condition.

INFORMATION has been received from Chihuahua, Mexico, of the extirpation of the Apache Chief Nana and his murdering band. Nana and some of his principal fighters were drawn up in line and shot by order of the Mexican authorities. The remainder of the band were sent to the City of Mexico, where they will be compelled to work in the mines for the remainder of their lives.

A SANGUINARY encounter is reported from Round Oak, Jones County, Ga. A young farmer named Jack Wm. Gray interfered with a negro dance and was fatally stabbed by three negro brothers, Bob, Henry and Aik Jackson. Gray fired into the brothers, killing all three, one dying on the spot, one before reaching the door, and the other a few hours later. Gray crawled out of the house and died on the steps.

He was taking a book from the shelf of his library, when he knocked down a pistol. The weapon struck the lower shelf and went off, the bullet entering the Professor's abdomen, passing through the bowels and lodging in the left hip. He died within twenty-four hours.

Forty or more students of the Keokuk (Iowa) Medical College have been taken down with small-pox, the result, as is believed, of handling a cadaver brought from Chicago for dissection. The college faculty admit that such a body was received, but say the disease was detected before it was placed upon the dissecting-table. The college has been quarantined by the Board of Health.

SMALL-POX in its most virulent form prevails in the vicinity of McCauleyville and Fort Abercrombie, Dakota Territory, and is spreading rapidly. The disease seems to be singularly fatal, some victims dying within twenty-four hours of the attack. It is said that before death blood gushes from the ears, eyes and nose of the patients. These symptoms suggest that the disease is not simple small-pox, but is in the nature of the plague.

THE County of Douglas, in Southern Dakota, was organized last winter, fraudulently, it is claimed, it having only about forty votes and some $12,000 of taxable property. It now transpires that some $200,000 in bonds have been issued by the officers of the county and put upon the Eastern market. Charles T. McCoy, a prominent politician of Bonhomme County, is supposed to be at the bottom of the fraud, and he has been arrested.

It is understood that the British Government has divided the disturbed portions of Ireland into five or six districts, each of which is to be under the supervision of a sort of magistrate, who will be able to act without previous superior sanction, and have entire control of troops and police, with a view to prompt action in the event of a disturbance. It is believed that this is a preliminary step toward the enforcement of the payment of rent. The City and County of Dublin and nine other counties have been proclaimed under the Arms act.

A DISPATCH from Augusta, Ga., 27th, says: Between 500 and 600 negroes from Edgefield County, South Carolina, passed through this city to-day on their way to Arkansas. They are under the leadership of a colored preacher named Hammond, who promised to have a chartered train waiting for them at Augusta, but failed to do so, and the party had to pay full rate to Atlanta. They say they found it too hard work to make a living in South Carolina, and determined to go elsewhere. Hammond went to Arkansas some time ago to examine the country, and on his return advised the negroes to go out there. It is expected 1,000 altogether will go.

Eson Bolin, his wife and four young children not long since emigrated from Stone County, Mo., to Benton County, Ark., taking up their residence at the village of Rogers. A few days ago Bolin was shot and killed while asleep in bed, and his wife was suspected of the murder, which she thereupon confessed, alleging as a justification therefor that he had frequently threatened her life, that he had murdered two men, was a horse-thief and a bad man generally. She was taken to Bentonville and lodged in jail to await trial, where after a few days' confinement she cut her throat from ear to ear, using for that purpose a knife which she had borrowed from the jailer for the ostensible purpose of ripping up a dress. Mrs. Bolin's maiden name was Johnson, and her mother, now Mrs. Gibson, and other relatives reside in Andrew County, Mo.

A SENSATIONAL episode in the Guiteau trial occurred on the 28th, when he was placed in the prisoner's dock, by order of the Court, on account of his persistent violation of order and decorum. In enforcing this decision Judge Cox said in effect that the extreme latitude hitherto permitted the prisoner had been for the purpose of affording the experts in court the fullest opportunity to judge of his mental and moral characteristics, and that the District-Attorney has expressly desired this freedom be granted the prisoner. The expert testimony being now about concluded, the Court said no further good could result from these unseen exhibitions of the prisoner, and he should therefore insist hereafter upon the orderly conduct of the case. Guiteau at first manifested the greatest renunciation to being removed to the prisoner's dock, promising to keep quiet if allowed to remain inside the bar. The order was, however, enforced, and the prisoner took his place in court for the first time as a common criminal.

Horrible.
One day last week one of the most horrible and outrageous affairs took place in the little village of Adairville, Ky.: Sambo Bailey, living about three miles from town, on the farm of Mr. Heck Hummers, went to Adairville. While there he took a drink or two of whiskey and got a little drunk, as he usually does when he goes to town. He attended to his business and started home. Mr. Allen Bell, an ex-Representative in the Tennessee Legislature, a big man in the church, who can pray louder and longer and jump up higher when praying than any other man we know of. Mr. Bell saw Sam Bailey when Sam was starting home, and remarked to him that if he didn't mind he would fall off his horse. Sambo said to Mr. Bell that it was none of his d—d business it he did fall off. He used some other indecent language at which Mr. Bell became offended, and satisfied his revengeful spirit by striking him (an eye witness says) one hundred lashes with his coat off. The whipping was done in the livery stable. Bell got Sam into the stable, and ordered every man out; but one remained, a respectable gentleman, who saw the whole affair. He describes it as

A HORRIBLE SIGHT.

He says he is willing to swear that Bell struck Sam one hundred lashes. There are marks on his person to show that he was whipped severely. One of his eyes is very nearly put out. The weapon used was a buggy whip.

There is considerable talk among the colored people about the affair, and almost every one, regardless of color or party, condemns the course of Bell as unlawful, ungentlemanly and unrefined.

On the other hand there are few old sor heads, full of prejudice and ignorance, who approve of Mr. Bell's course. They are not yet realized that tails Negro is free and equal before the law.—Commercial.

CHRISTMAS DIVERSIONS.
Two Negroes Killed and a Nymph Badly Bombarded.
While Christmas is generally acknowledged to be a season of good cheer and happy reunion—a time at which we forget past differences and all meet for thanksgiving and general rejoicing, there are those who seem to think that unless they do some desperate deed on that day they have not fully commemorated it. Last Saturday and Sunday's pleasure in Waco and surroundings was somewhat marred among the colored people and demimonde by acts of violence which add none to the credit and good standing of the participants and may get all concerned into serious trouble. The first scene of blood we heard of was the finding of the body of a negro on the railroad track near Reagan. What his name was we could not learn, but have been informed that two trains passed over him. It is further stated that he was seen to have a bundle of clothes and was known to have money, all of which was missing when the body was found. It is thought that he was killed by some unknown parties and his remains placed upon the track as a blind to cover their villainy. Following this news comes the announcement that two Waco members of the demi-monde enlivened Christmas and the holy Sabbath morning by indulging in an unusual discussion. It occurred at the apartments of Mabel Clark, on Jackson street, and Nellie Cunningham figures as the principal actress. Some time just before noon it appears she had taken morning drams enough to wake up all the meanness there was in those she had the night before, and having nothing else to do took a pistol and made an unprovoked assault on Mabel, who, being defenseless, had to stand and wait for her to empty the pistol, which, it is said, she did in brief order. After she had satisfied her shooting propensity she retired to her room and barred the doors. When the police arrived she refused them admission, and a complaint had to be made by Mabel before they felt they had proper authority to break into the house. In the meantime the police got in and secured her by strategy. She is now in the county jail. The other woman was not injured. At the time the woman did the shooting she is said to have been very drunk and no doubt had not the least knowledge of what she was doing. By the way of a wind up one Nath. Williams, as he is called, who is said to have manipulated cat-gut at the dollar store for the edification of callers, put out the light of another negro, Bob Graves, on the John Bedwell place, about five miles below town. It occurred, as we learn, about 3 o'clock Sunday evening. Particulars as to the cause are meager, and to a large extent unreliable. Some say that all the darkeyes were drunk. Williams himself, who was caught yesterday morning, states that Graves siped him in the face before shot him, and others were credited with having said they heard Williams say he was going to shoot him just to see him kick. A courier came to town after an officer and Deputy Sheriff George Oglesby at once went down and spent most of the night trailing him with the bloodhounds. He had a great deal of trouble getting on his trail after he crossed Tehuacana, but before daylight got the dogs in good chase. The negro, finding himself hotly pursued, at last returned to the scene of the killing and gave himself up. Sheriff Van Hall happened to be on the ground and conducted him to jail. Such scenes sadly mar the Christmms festivities and do not speak in good terms for the participants, though all sensible people will not blame communities for the acts of individuals on such occasions.

Lawlessness in Texas.
BLOODY WORK IN ORANGE
St. Louis, August 23. — The Republican's special from Houston, Texas, received last night, gives particulars of the bloody tragedies, which have occurred at Orange during the week past, and which have been previously mentioned. They have caused intense excitement along the line of the Texas & New Orleans railroad, and fears are entertained that something worse is to follow. The citizens of Orange have risen en masse and are determined to end the reign of lawlessness that has prevailed for the past month. The present condition of affairs grew out of a difficulty which occurred three weeks ago between O. L. Delano, a noted desperado, and a detective named Wood, in which Delano was seriously shot. Wood escaped, and Charles Delano, a brother of O. L., accused the sheriff, Geo. Michael, of aiding in the escape, and swore he would get even with him. With this view he concocted a plan to assassinate Michael, and was aided by Dug Harris and two negroes, Sam and Bob Saxon. The plan failed, but they succeeded in very seriously wounding the sheriff by leading him into an ambush. The citizens became greatly incensed at these proceedings, and 150 of them congregated, captured four of the negroes and shot them. Bob Saxon was also captured, and after extorting a confession from him, in which he reviewed the plot to kill the sheriff and gave much other information, he was hanged to a tree. Another negro was arrested and hanged, and Chas. Delano was captured and placed in jail. A hundred armed men scoured the neighboring swamps for others of the gang.

Texas Topics.

SERIOUS SHOOTING AFFRAY.

GALVESTON, TEX., August 23. — The News has the following specials: Graham, Texas. — A serious shooting affray occurred yesterday in Belknap, between a merchant named Ben Donnel, and a blacksmith, in which the latter was shot twice in the abdomen and once in the shoulder, and probably mortally wounded. The blacksmith was intoxicated, and Donnel claims to have shot him in self defence.
LOST IN A FLOOD IN THE RIO GRANDE.
A special to the News, from Eagle Pass, Texas, says: The Rio Grande has been unusually high for some time, and has been unnavigable by small boats. It having gone down considerably, yesterday a ferry boat was put out, but on reaching the middle of the stream a tremendous rush of water threatened to swamp the boat. The ferryman cut the rope which held the boat, but the boat was rapidly carried down the river by the merciless torrent. It is feared that all on board, numbering five, were lost.

A BODY MUTILATED BY WILD HOGS.
A special to the News from Beaumont, Texas, says:—The body of John Mahoney, found in the weeds near here, was so horribly mutilated by wild hogs as to be almost unrecognizable.

OUTRAGE BY A ONE LEGGED NEGRO.
SAN ANTONIO, TEXAS, August 22.—A one legged negro was arrested to-day for committing an outrage upon the person of a young German girl, while she was on her way home from mass, first knocking the girl down with his crutch and rendering her insensible. The negro was arrested and lodged in jail before his crime was generally known, else it is thought he would have been summarily dealt with.
sam-saxon-orange-1881-08-17.A8:
BLOODY WORK. Eight Texas Desperadoes Lynched.
HOUSTON, TEXAS, Aug. 23.—Eight desperadoes have been lynched at Orange. It was the comparatively sober act of an organized band of citizens who determined to rid the county of a murderous gang of outlaws. The immediate cause was an attack of the gang on Sheriff George Michel.

One of the gang, O. L. Delano, attempted to escape from jail and was shot by Deputy Wood. The rest of the gang went to jail and demanded that Wood be given up. The sheriff was overpowered, the jail searched, and Wood was not found. He had been removed to a safe place. The gang, believing they had been deceived by the sheriff, threatened the latter's life.

The jail guard was increased, and the gang made futile efforts to get at the sheriff. They then began a series of outrages intended to draw the sheriff out of the jail, so they could attack him. Yesterday four of them, Charles Delano and "Dug" Harris, White, and "Sam" and "Bob" Saxon, colored, made a sham fight, cleaned out the saloon and burned the building.

The sheriff started for them, and followed "Bob" Saxon into a trap behind a covered fence, when a volley was fired, and Michel fell wounded with buckshot in many places. He was covered with blood. The gang believed they had killed him, and fled. Michel is now unconscious, and at the jail he is believed to be dying. The whole town rose up; a public meeting was held, and it was unanimously voted to lynch the gang, and a committee of 150 was appointed for that purpose. Early this morning four of the negroes were caught and shot in a field without preliminaries.

Robert Garzon, a colored leader, was captured and a confession was demanded and refused. He was hung to a tree until he was unconscious, and then taken down and resuscitated and was stretched five times before he made a full confession. He was then hanged a sixth time until he was dead. Finding they were right as to the men they had hanged and shot, and of others whom they suspected, they captured Sam Saxon and Charles Delano and put them in jail.

After a consultation it was decided to hang them, and they were taken into the street. While ropes were being procured they attempted to escape, and were shot, and their bodies were left bleeding in the roadway. O. L. Delano was then brought out and formally tried by Judge Lynch. He was dragged down the road with a rope about his neck and hanged to a telegraph pole.
sam-saxon-orange-1881-08-17.A31:
Sheriff Michael Shot.
Orange was brown into intense excitement Wednesday night by the shooting of George W. Michael, our brave and gallant sheriff; and the killing and hanging which followed as a natural result of the rage and indignation of the community. To give minute details of the affair is impossible at this writing, but below we present a brief and as accurate a statement as possible.

Shortly after dark, Sam. Saxon, colored, and two or three other negroes made an assault upon a white man, Gus Garvey, in the Sample Room Saloon, several shots being fired. It seems that Saxon had threatened to shoot Garvey early in the evening and that the latter had purchased a shot gun to defend himself, but from some cause did not use his gun successfully. No one was hurt by the shooting. Sheriff Michael and deputy Ferguson were close by and started immediately in pursuit of the negroes, being joined by three or four others. When the posse reached a point just beyond Mr. A. Gilmer's residence and near negro town, they ran suddenly upon the negroes, who, it appears, were lying in ambush, and in an instant the posse was fired into, a shotgun charge taking effect in Mr. Michael's right arm and side. The posse fired, shooting Sam Saxon and another negro down, the others escaping. It was then discovered that the sheriff was dangerously hurt; news to the effect reached town, and in five or ten minutes at least one hundred and fifty citizens were in arms and in pursuit of the negroes. They were excited, and believing at the time that the sheriff was mortally wounded, left no stone unturned to capture the whole gang. Their success manifested itself the next morning in the shape of Robert Saxon, a brother of Sam's, hanging to the large oak in front of D. Call & Son's store, two others killed and a number wounded. We should state just here that Sam Saxon, after the shooting at the saloon, ran with his crowd out towards negro town, where he was joined by a num-
some discoveries the next morning caused a suspicion that the whole affair was a deep laid plan to kill the sheriff and deputy, and warrants were issued for the arrest of several white men as the originators, one of them being Charlie Delano, who was promptly arrested and placed in jail. Several negroes were also arrested, as accessories, and jailed. The Rifles were called out early in the morning by Captain Norsworthy, and kept on duty all day guarding the prisoners. — [Orange (Texas) Tribune, Aug. 19.
sam-saxon-orange-1881-08-17.A32:
The Rioting in Orange.
[Special Correspondence to the Galveston News, Aug. 22.]
The rioting in Orange still continues and the wildest excitement prevails. About 8 o'clock last night the Orange Rifles, considering everything quiet and there being no visible signs of any intended outbreak, disbanded and returned to their homes, leaving the jail unguarded. About one hour later an armed party of citizens surrounded the jail and demanded its surrender. Deputy Sheriff Rance Jett, who was in charge, seeing that it was useless to contend with the overpowering force yielded up the jail. The invaders at once entered and took out Sam Saxon, the ringleader of the negro desperados, and another negro, said to be an accomplice. Saxon is the negro who escaped after the affray last week, but was so closely pursued by his hunters that he came up on Sunday morning and gave himself up and was placed in the jail for safe-keeping. Upon being taken out of the jail by the mob, Saxon's courage failed him, and he dropped on his knees at the deputy sheriff's feet, and throwing his armis around Sheriff Jett's legs, implored God's mercy upon his soul. Recognizing that all hope was gone, and that they were to be killed, Saxon and the other negro became frantic in their efforts to escape, and their terrifying yells of "murder" could be heard at a great distance. The exasperated citizens endeavored to quiet them, but to no avail, and at once filled their bodies full of buckshot. A general stampede was made by the congregations of the various churches, which were at worship, and the ministers fled their churches without a benediction.

Some startling confessions were made by Saxon before his death. He testified that he had been paid by Charles Delano to steal a carload of cattle last fall from the Louisiana Western Railroad, and that a certain woman connected with the desperadoes had offered him $500 to burn the town, that the spoils of a plot to which she was a party, might be reaped by herself and confederates. He attempted to accomplish this end but failed, only succeeding in burning one house and store, last fall.

A trial of Charles Delano was to have taken place at 9 o'clock this morning, at which Judge Lynch was to preside, and it is probable that by this time his neck will have been broken. Many of his accomplices are still at large, including his four brothers-in-law, the Harrises, and Ol. Delano and two negroes, but they are being trailed down and will, in all probability, be captured and suffer the penalty inflicted by an enraged community.

The latest news from Orange is that Delano, on being admitted to bail, secured his bondsmen against loss, and left Orange county, with several of his male relatives, apparently forever. Everything is quiet at Orange now.
sam-saxon-orange-1881-08-17.A38:
Terror's Reign in Texas Dispatch to the Globe-Democrat
HOUSTON, Texas, August 25.—A meeting of 300 of the leading colored people of Galveston yesterday, and which called attention to the bloody outrages perpetrated on negroes at Orange by an armed mob of white citizens, and denouncing Governor Roberts and the state government for declining to interfere, has aroused a still higher degree of public interest in the late wholesale lynching in this state. The Galveston News is the leading paper in Texas, and several days ago called upon the state government to interfere and stop this dreadful slaughter of human beings, who were utterly helpless in the hands of a mob; but Governor Roberts has remained utterly silent. The facts of the whole business are that for six years a feud has existed between two parties at Orange, one composed of citizens of the town and its young white men, and the other of male members of two or three leading families in the surrounding country—the Harrises and others. Chas. Delano, the alleged leader of the opposition party, is a white man of 35, and married into the Harris family. He is a stock raiser and cattle man, and his followers, called by the citizens of Orange his gang, include, besides his kinsmen, some eight or ten negroes, two of them named Robert and Sam Saxon, mulates, and reputed sons of one of the prominent white citizens of the vicinity. As stated in the dispatch, Bob Saxon was hung in Wednesday's riot of last week, and his brother Sam was shot dead by a mob last Sunday night. Latterly Charles Delano was regarded as the leader of the Saxon, or negro, party, and Sheriff Michael of that of the citizens, and for months past a difficulty was expected. All sorts of crimes have been laid to the charge of the Saxon party, among them the robbery of the express agent at Orange by two masked men, and a short time ago the theft of cattle. Of course the citizens' party only waited for a chance at their opponents, and got it, but in the riot last week, when Sheriff Michael was shot, it has not been established, as stated by Michael's party, that the Saxon party were the first to fire on him, or that there was an ambush of negroes waiting to assassinate the sheriff, as claimed. Mrs. Delano, whom Sam Saxon

charged with hiring him for $500 to burn the town, is a lady with spirit and influence enough with her relatives to stir up a movement for revenge in case her husband is hung, as has been threatened by the lynchers. It is not believed that the friends of the Saxons will let the matter rest, but the reign of terror now existing in Orange may change into a reign of assassination. Persons who saw the shooting of the two negro prisoners taken from the Orange jail on Sunday night, say it was most horrible and brutally. The cries of the poor wretches were pitiful as they clung to the knees of the officers for protection, in the face of a mob of thirty men, but they were shot down like dogs. Orange is now completely at the mercy of the mob, who hung one negro and shot four others to death without a semblance of a trial. Delano's friends assert he had nothing to do with inciting the negroes to fire at Sheriff Michael.

ODD SHIPMENTS BY EXPRESS.

Babies, Bears Snakes, and Other Queer Articles of Freight.

"Odd freight? Well, I should say we have," said R. F. Masters, one of the oldest clerks in the main office of the Adams express company, on Market street, as he twirled himself around on his high stool and faced an inquiring reporter yesterday afternoon. Mr. Masters talks with great volubility, and, as he has a habit of dropping many small words, his conversation was decidedly jerky. "Yes, we ship a little of everything, from diamonds to Chester white pigs and Limberg cheese. Remarkable thing about that cheese. Ever smell any? Rich, penetrating sort of fragrance, ain't it? Case burst in freight room last spring. Made every one sick. Two Irishmen tried to shovel it up. Smell nearly turned 'em inside out. Got a Dutchman, regular out-and-out eat-a-sandwich-in-a-minute sort of a fellow, from Bergmyer's saloon across the way, but he gave out in ten minutes. Only finished it with a box of deodorizer. Phew! They should charge double rates to ship such stuff," and the speaker elevated his nose as though a trace of the diabolical aroma still lingered in his nostrils.

"Two babies have come through this office, one from Chicago for New York and the other from Washington to this city. The men on this line made a great fuss when the Chicago young one was shipped. Telegraph operators all along the route sent dispatches ahead and crowds of people went to the depots to see the baby. Came all the way in the express cars. Had a hammock rigged up. New idea, you know, and messengers thought it was a kind of a joke, but they wouldn't like too much work of that kind. Baby's mother died in Chicago, father lived in New York; weighed forty-one pounds, I believe; cost about two dollars and a half to send it through. Philadelphia baby came along some time after. Both made their trip first-class, and seemed to enjoy things generally. Fed 'em on regular spoon victuals from hotels along the line. Ofted have dead folks shipped. Don't know why they should send them by express tho', 'Tain't likely ane one's going to walk off with a corpse. Yes, a man shipped three Short-horn cattle clean through to Nebraska about a month ago. Unless he got 'em for nothing, they must have cost him a power of money when he got them. Just think of a man expressing a whole deer carcass two or three thousand miles. About as sensible for a butcher to express a beef through from here to Camden. Last fall a lunatic sent a twelve hundred pound block of cedar from California to New York. That's nothing, however, for I see some one sent twenty barrels of mess pork to the Pottstown military camp by express, and the charges amounted to over $100. A cinnamon bear came through from Nevada by express last January for the Zoological Garden. Said he was tame when they shipped him. Got loose near Omaha, drove every one out of car, chewed up half a deer, ripened among the freight and had a circus all to himself until he was lassoed and tied in a corner of the car with log chains. Oh, yes, they ship lots of mirrors, but the men don't like 'em. Seven years' bad luck to smash a looking-glass, you know. Snakes till you can't rest, but they keep them in boxes. Messengers don't mind 'em. Now you might think eggs are a nice freight, but they ain't. More expressmen grow bald on account of worrying over baskets of eggs than anything I know of," and Mr. Masters turned from the reporter to receive a package of hymn books consigned to a missionary among the Black Hills.
sam-saxon-orange-1881-08-17.A39:
The End at Orange-A Lame and Impotent Conclusion.
Since our last record two other negroes were killed by the mob at Orange. One of them voluntarily give himself up, and the same day was murdered. Before his death he gave information most clearly criminating Delano, the white leader of the band, who was in jail, and certain white confederates of his, persons who on account their wealth had heretofore defied justice. The negro stated that the wife of one of them had offered him $500. to burn the town. Yet in the face of all this Delano was not only not lynched, not only not brought to prompt trial, but was actually admitted to bail in the sum of $2000. on his promise to leave the country. We copy the just comments from the Houston Post:
The unexpected clemency of the people in reference to Delano, a notorious criminal, excites surprise and severe comment. Negroes who surrendered were shot down, but the ring-leader of the band, for some unexplained reason, is permitted to give bond and to leave the country. It is true we are not exactly in a position to judge of the policy of this extraordinary action of the Orange people. It is probable that they have adopted this method of getting rid of a bad character with his family and accomplices as the most obvious and easy of execution. But, in doing so, it should be borne in mind that they have left themselves under a reproach of compounding felony and something even worse, immediately upon the heels of a passionate breach of the law in the summary execution of Saxon and his companion. This is unfortunate in the last degree. The exigency of the occasion, the turbulence and excitement of the people may possibly be plead in extenuation for the precipitate action in reference to the killing of the negroes, though they cannot justify the violence. But the deliberate interference with the procedure of justice in the case of Delano, who should have been indicted for larceny, arson and murder, and his being turned loose upon the general community with the accusation of these crimes accompanying him wherever he goes, is an act not only indefensible but monstrous. We do not see how the people of Orange can defend their action in the premises. To be sure, they may thereby make a short-cut to the peace and order they so much desire, but the method by which this desirable end is obtained is both an illegal and an unmanly one. Why should they discriminate between Saxon, the tool, and Delano, the instigator? Why should Orange rid herself of a criminal citizen at the expense of the people at large?
